title: How do palaeontologists work?
text: Palaeontologists are scientists who study life from the distant past. They work a bit like detectives: they cannot see the dinosaurs, so they must find clues in fossils and rocks.

The work often starts in deserts or cliffs, where old rock layers are visible. When palaeontologists find a bone, they dig very slowly with small tools and brushes. A big skeleton can take months or even years to remove. Then they cover the bones with plaster to protect them during the trip to the museum.

Fossils tell many stories. Big footprints in a line might show that a dinosaur was walking alone. Many footprints together could mean that the animals lived in groups. If a skull has teeth like knives, the animal must have been a meat eater.

Sometimes the clues are surprising. Some fossils show feathers, so scientists now think that many dinosaurs might have been colorful. A dinosaur found sitting on its eggs must have protected its babies like a bird.

Of course, palaeontologists cannot be completely sure about everything. New discoveries can change old ideas. That is what makes this science so exciting: the next fossil might rewrite the history of life on Earth.

grammar.title: Grammar: modals of deduction
grammar.rule: Use must when you are almost sure something is true, might or could when it is possible, and cannot when you are sure it is not true.
rows: It must be a meat eater.
It could mean they lived in groups.
items: With teeth like knives, it ___ be a meat eater.
We are not sure, but it ___ be colorful.
It has no feathers, so it ___ be a bird.
Many footprints together ___ mean a group.
It was sitting on its eggs: it must have ___ its babies.
